summary: Describes ACTN, a framework for abstracting and controlling traffic-engineered networks. It builds on the separation of data and control planes and the many management protocols, so that customers and controllers can see and drive virtual, abstracted views of underlying networks.

plainLanguage.summary: Abstraction and Control of Traffic-Engineered Networks (ACTN) lets a customer request a virtual network across one or more networks. Controllers translate the request into network configuration while showing only the topology information allowed by policy.

subtitle: A framework for presenting customers with abstracted virtual views of traffic-engineered networks.

tldr.problem: Customers need virtual network services across multiple technology and administrative domains without directly controlling each underlying network.
tldr.mechanism: ACTN defines Customer Network Controllers, a Multi-Domain Service Coordinator, Provisioning Network Controllers, and interfaces that exchange requests and abstracted topology.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8453 is an Informational framework that defines architecture and terms, not specific protocols; it records no IANA actions.

facts.label: ACTN interfaces
facts.value: CMI and MPI; SBI is out of scope

today: RFC 8453 is Informational, and the batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It provides a framework and terminology for ACTN rather than defining its protocols.

sections.title: What ACTN Is For
sections.content:
A traffic-engineered network uses a connection-oriented technology and a control plane to provision end-to-end connectivity. Abstraction and Control of TE Networks (ACTN) describes management and control functions that build virtual networks from underlying network resources.

A virtual link shown to a customer may be formed from one or more paths in the provider's networks. The framework supports abstraction, virtualization, network slicing, and coordination across domains and technology layers.
sections.plainLanguage: ACTN describes how providers can offer customers a virtual network built from real network resources. The customer can work with the virtual view instead of each underlying network.

sections.title: Virtual Networks and Services
sections.content:
A Virtual Network (VN) is a network offered to a customer as if it were physical. A Type 1 VN is a set of edge-to-edge links; a Type 2 VN is a topology of virtual nodes and links. Type 1 is a special case of Type 2.

A Virtual Network Service (VNS) is the agreement between a customer and operator. In a Type 1 service the customer can create and operate the VN. A Type 2a topology is created at service setup and cannot be changed by the customer; Type 2b allows dynamic topology changes.
sections.plainLanguage: A customer can receive a set of virtual links or a virtual network map. The service agreement determines whether the customer can change that map.

sections.title: Controllers and Interfaces
sections.content:
The Customer Network Controller (CNC) communicates service requirements. The Multi-Domain Service Coordinator (MDSC) coordinates domains, abstracts resources, maps customer requests, and coordinates virtual services. The Provisioning Network Controller (PNC) configures network elements and gathers topology information.

The CNC-MDSC Interface (CMI) carries customer service requests. The MDSC-PNC Interface (MPI) carries connectivity and bandwidth requests and presents abstracted topology. The Southbound Interface (SBI) between a PNC and network elements is outside the scope of ACTN. Implementations may collocate functional components or use a hierarchy of MDSCs.
sections.plainLanguage: The customer controller sends its needs to a coordinator, and network controllers configure resources. Two defined interfaces connect these roles; the device-facing interface is outside this framework.

sections.title: Topology Abstraction
sections.content:
The PNC or a lower-level MDSC can present an abstract topology. The level of detail depends on network policy, technology, controller capability, scalability, and confidentiality needs.

A native or white topology exposes the actual network. A black topology represents a whole domain as one abstract node. A grey topology exposes border nodes and some abstract connectivity; type A uses a full mesh of TE links, while type B includes more internal abstract nodes and links. Grey topology can be generated by configuration or supplemented through path-computation requests.
sections.plainLanguage: A controller can reveal the full topology, hide a domain behind one abstract node, or show a partial map. Policy determines how much detail another controller receives.

sections.title: Multi-Destination Services
sections.content:
ACTN can support a service where the network chooses among possible destinations based on network conditions. The CNC provides candidate source and destination access points and service constraints; the MDSC coordinates with PNCs to select a destination and set up connectivity.

The customer may request a backup destination or ask for a new destination when network conditions change. Actions after the MDSC reports a selected endpoint, such as application orchestration, are outside the scope of ACTN.
sections.plainLanguage: A customer can provide several possible destinations and let the MDSC choose one using network conditions and service constraints. The framework can also describe backup or later destination changes.

sections.title: Management and Security
sections.content:
ACTN management includes external and internal interfaces, component monitoring, and policy configuration. Policies may set connectivity, bandwidth, route, technology, security, resilience, or cost constraints. The RFC discusses policy examples but does not mandate a policy enforcement method.

Requests, resource control, confidentiality, and availability are security concerns. The RFC recommends considering encryption between components, authentication and authorization for CNC access, and trusted connections between MDSCs and PNCs. It leaves protocol-specific security details to use-case documents.
sections.plainLanguage: ACTN needs policies for which services customers may request and how resources are used. Controllers should authenticate one another and protect sensitive network and customer information.
